title: Fire alarm in a training centre
audience: Trainee: rescuer or junior officer on duty
context: Educational, non-combat civil-protection scenario. No weapons, harm or combat content.

steps.title: The alarm sounds
steps.situation: 14:20. The fire alarm sounds in a four-storey training centre. You are the duty officer on the second floor with twelve people. There is a faint smell of smoke from the north stairwell, and everyone looks at you for direction.
steps.question: What is your first instruction?

options.text: Stay where you are until the alarm is confirmed as real.
Everyone leaves now by the stairs, taking only what they can carry in a few seconds.
First collect documents and equipment from the offices.

steps.why: Treating the alarm as real, using the stairs and not delaying for belongings keeps the group safe.
steps.hint: Think about what an alarm means until it is officially confirmed otherwise, and how a group should leave a building.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: The fire alarm sounded at 14:20 in a four-storey training centre. You are the duty officer on the second floor with twelve people, there is a faint smell of smoke from the north stairwell, and the group is waiting for your instruction.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: Section S1, Responding to an alarm, covers what to do when an alarm sounds and how to leave the building. You can read it in full from the source chip below before you decide.

chat.question: What if someone needs help to move?
chat.answer: The guide says to help people who need assistance only if it is safe. Otherwise, report where they are to responders so trained people can reach them.

chat.question: Why not take the elevator?
chat.answer: Elevators can stop or fill with smoke during a fire, which can trap the group. The guide is clear: during a fire, use the stairs.

chat.question: Why not wait until the alarm is confirmed?
chat.answer: The guide asks you to treat every alarm as real until it is officially confirmed otherwise. Waiting costs time, and in this situation smoke is already spreading.

chat.question: Can people take their things?
chat.answer: Only what they can carry in a few seconds. The guide says never to delay your exit to collect belongings, documents or equipment.

steps.title: Is it only a test?
steps.situation: The group is starting to stand up when a colleague says the building ran a fire test last month and this is probably just another one. Nobody has announced anything yet, and the alarm keeps sounding.
steps.question: What do you tell the group?

options.text: It is probably a test, so wait a few minutes for an announcement.
Keep working until someone confirms there is a fire.
Treat it as real and keep leaving until it is officially confirmed otherwise.

steps.why: The guide says to treat every alarm as real until it is officially confirmed otherwise. A guess that it is only a test is not a confirmation.
steps.hint: Think about what counts as a confirmation, and whether a guess is enough.

steps.title: One last task
steps.situation: The group is on its feet, but one participant is still typing the last lines of a report and says it will only take a minute. Others have stopped to watch what you do.
steps.question: What do you say?

options.text: Stop now and join the group; the report is not essential.
Finish the sentence quickly, then follow us.
Save the report and shut the computer down properly before leaving.

steps.why: The guide says to stop non-essential tasks when the alarm sounds. A report that can wait is a non-essential task.
steps.hint: Ask yourself whether the task has to be done before anyone can leave safely.

steps.title: What to carry
steps.situation: At the door, people reach for their things. One person picks up a small bag from the chair beside them, while another starts to unplug a projector and gather the training equipment from the table.
steps.question: What do you tell them about their belongings?

options.text: Leave everything behind, even small personal items.
Take whatever you need, as long as everyone leaves together.
Take only what you can carry in a few seconds and leave the rest.

steps.why: The guide says to take only what you can carry in a few seconds. Gathering equipment would slow the whole group down.
steps.hint: Think about how long picking something up should take.

steps.title: The forgotten coat

steps.question: What do you tell them?

options.text: Do not go back; keep moving to the exit.
Go back quickly, as it is close, and catch up.
Ask a colleague to fetch the things while the rest wait.

steps.why: The guide says never to delay your exit to collect belongings, even when they are close by.
steps.hint: Consider how a short detour changes the way the whole group leaves.

steps.title: The elevator

steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: Let the people who are tired use the elevator while the others take the stairs.
Tell them to wait at the elevator until its doors open.
Direct everyone to the stairs, not the elevator.

steps.why: The guide says not to use elevators during a fire and to use the stairs instead.
steps.hint: Think about which way of moving between floors the guide allows during a fire.

steps.title: Someone needs help
steps.situation: As the group heads for the stairs, a visitor who walks with crutches tells you they cannot manage the stairs quickly. The corridor is still clear.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: Send the visitor down in the elevator on their own.
Have a colleague help the visitor down the stairs if it is safe, and if not, make sure their exact location is reported to responders.
Tell the visitor to wait in an office until the alarm stops.

steps.why: The guide says to help people who need assistance only if it is safe, and otherwise to report where they are so responders can reach them.
steps.hint: Think about how to keep the whole group moving while still looking after the person who needs help.

chat.answer: A visitor who walks with crutches has told you they cannot move quickly. The corridor is still clear, and the rest of your group is waiting for direction.

chat.answer: Section S1, Responding to an alarm, covers how to react to an alarm and how to leave. S4 covers the assembly point and what to tell the people in charge there.

chat.answer: Only what they can carry in a few seconds. The guide says never to delay your exit to collect belongings.

chat.question: Why not use the elevator for the visitor?
chat.answer: Elevators can stop or fill with smoke during a fire, which could trap the visitor alone. The guide says to use the stairs.

chat.question: Why not stop the group until the visitor is ready?
chat.answer: Holding everyone back delays the exit for the whole group. The guide's approach is to help the person only if it is safe, keep the others moving, and report the person's location if they cannot get out.

chat.question: Why not let the visitor wait in an office?
chat.answer: Waiting alone in an office keeps the visitor in danger, and nobody would know where they are. If they cannot leave, responders need their exact location.

Keep helping the visitor down despite the smoke.
Stay with the visitor and wait for the alarm to be switched off.

steps.why: The guide says to help people who need assistance only if it is safe, and otherwise to report their location to responders.

steps.title: A hot door
steps.situation: The nearest exit is the north stairwell. You touch its door with the back of your hand and it feels hot.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: Wait next to the door for responders.
Open it slowly to see what is behind it.
Keep it closed and lead the group to the south stairwell.

steps.why: A hot door means you should not open it. Another route keeps the group away from the fire.
steps.hint: A closed door can hide a fire on the other side. Think about what you learn before you open anything.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: The nearest exit is on the north side of the building. You checked its door with the back of your hand and it felt hot. The twelve people are with you in the corridor.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: Section S2, Checking the route, covers how to check a door before going through it and how to use doors as you move. S3 covers moving through smoke.

chat.question: How do I check a door?
chat.answer: Before going through a door, feel it with the back of your hand. The guide uses that check to decide whether the route behind it is safe to use.

chat.question: Why not open the door slowly to look?
chat.answer: A hot door suggests fire or heat on the other side. Opening it, even slowly, can let fire and smoke into your corridor. Opening slowly and being ready to shut it again is the guide's advice only for a door that feels cool.

chat.question: Why not wait by the door for responders?
chat.answer: Staying next to a hot door keeps the group close to the heat and to smoke that can come through. The guide says to use another route.

chat.question: Would opening it let the smoke out?
chat.answer: No. Opening the door lets in air that can feed the fire and pushes smoke into your route.

image.alt: A closed office door in a corridor that a person is about to open

steps.title: Smoke in the corridor
steps.situation: The corridor to the south stairwell has a thin layer of smoke along the ceiling. The group is nervous.
steps.question: How do you move the group?

options.text: Move low, cover nose and mouth, keep a hand on the wall and close doors behind you.
Run upright to get there before the smoke thickens.
Go back and shelter in an office with the door open.

steps.why: Staying low keeps you in cleaner air, the wall keeps your direction and closed doors slow the spread of smoke.
steps.hint: Smoke and hot gases rise. Think about where the cleaner air is and how to keep your direction.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: The corridor to the south stairwell has a thin layer of smoke along the ceiling. The group is nervous and looking to you.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: Section S3, Moving through smoke, covers how smoke behaves and how to move through it. S2, Checking the route, is also linked to this step.

chat.question: Why not run upright?
chat.answer: Smoke and hot gases rise, so moving upright puts people in the worst air. Staying low keeps them in cleaner air near the floor.

chat.question: Why not break a window?
chat.answer: Extra air can make a fire grow, and breaking a window will not clear the corridor. The guide says not to break windows to clear smoke from a corridor.

chat.question: Why not shelter in an office?
chat.answer: Sheltering with the door open lets smoke follow you in and takes the group away from the exit. If a route is truly blocked, the guide's advice is a room with a window, with the door closed and gaps sealed, and then signalling and calling for help.

steps.title: A colleague is hurt
steps.situation: At the south landing a colleague sits against the wall, conscious and talking. A deep cut on the forearm is bleeding heavily, and there is also a small burn on the hand. The landing is clear of smoke.
steps.question: What do you do first?

options.text: Cool the burn under running water.
Lift the cloth every minute to check whether the bleeding has stopped.
Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth and keep the pressure on.

steps.why: Firm direct pressure is the first step to control severe bleeding.
steps.hint: Think about which injury threatens life first, and what stops the loss of blood.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: At the south landing a colleague is sitting against the wall, conscious and talking. A deep cut on the forearm is bleeding heavily, and there is a small burn on the hand. The landing is clear of smoke.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: S6, Assessing an injured person, covers checking the scene and the person and deciding what to deal with first. S7 covers severe bleeding and S8 covers burns.

chat.question: Is it safe to stop on the landing?
chat.answer: The guide says to check that the scene is safe first, so you do not become a second casualty. Here the landing is described as clear of smoke.

chat.question: Why treat the bleeding before the burn?
chat.answer: Severe bleeding is life-threatening, and the guide says to deal with life-threatening problems first. The burn can be cooled once the bleeding is under control.

chat.question: Why not lift the cloth to check?
chat.answer: Lifting the cloth releases the pressure and can restart the bleeding. If the cloth soaks through, the guide says to add more layers on top instead of removing it.

chat.question: How should the burn be treated later?
chat.answer: Cool it under cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, oils or toothpaste, do not burst blisters, and cover it loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing. A burn on the hand is a reason to seek medical help.

steps.title: Calling for help
steps.situation: You are holding pressure on the wound. Three people from the group stand nearby, and nobody has called for help yet.
steps.question: How do you get help on the way?

options.text: Say loudly: "Someone call 112."
Point at one person: "You, call 112, report one casualty with severe bleeding and our location, then tell me what they said."
Release the pressure and call yourself.

steps.why: A named person with clear details and a report-back makes sure the call happens.
steps.hint: A call for help aimed at everyone often goes unanswered. Think about who is responsible, and what responders need to hear.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: You are holding pressure on your colleague's wound. Three people from the group are standing nearby, and nobody has called for help yet.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: Section S5, Calling for help, covers the emergency number, what to say on the call and how to make sure a call is made.

chat.question: Which number should be called?
chat.answer: The guide uses 112 or the local emergency number.

chat.question: Why point at one specific person?
chat.answer: A general request makes everyone assume someone else has already called. Naming one person, and asking them to report back, makes sure the call actually happens.

chat.question: Why not stop and call myself?
chat.answer: Stopping pressure on a severe bleed lets it start again. Keep pressing and delegate the call.

chat.question: What should the caller say?
chat.answer: Give the location, what happened, the number of injured people and any hazards, then stay on the line until told to hang up.

steps.title: Assembly point
steps.situation: You and your colleague, with pressure still applied, reach the assembly point. The headcount shows that one person from your group is missing. Paramedics arrive.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: Go back inside to look for the missing person.
Wait quietly until someone asks you.
Tell responders the missing person's name and last known location, then hand over the casualty: what happened, what you did and when.

steps.why: Clear information to responders is the fastest way to help the missing person and the casualty.
steps.hint: Responders need specific facts about anyone missing. Think about what to pass on, and to whom.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: You and your colleague have reached the assembly point with pressure still applied. The headcount shows that one person from your group is missing, and paramedics are arriving.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: S4, Assembly point and headcount, covers what to do once you are out of the building. S10 covers the handover to the people who take over.

chat.question: Why is the assembly point away from the entrances?
chat.answer: The guide places it away from the building and its entrances so emergency teams can get in and work without people in their way.

chat.question: Why not go back in to look?
chat.answer: The guide says not to re-enter the building until responders declare it safe. The fastest help for the missing person is giving responders their name and last known location.

chat.question: What goes into a good handover?
chat.answer: A short, ordered handover: what happened, what you found, what you did and when, and any changes since. Name any missing person and the last place they were seen.

chat.question: Why not send someone else in?
chat.answer: Sending someone back in puts another person at risk and gives responders a second person to look for. Leave the search to them.

steps.title: A cool door
steps.situation: With pressure still applied, you and your colleague reach the bottom of the south stairwell. A shut door leads to the ground-floor lobby and the exit. You check it with the back of your hand: it is cool.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: Open it slowly, ready to close it at once if you see smoke or feel heat.
Open it wide and send everyone through at a run.
Leave it shut and take the group back upstairs to look for another route.

steps.why: A cool door can be opened, but slowly and with care, so you can shut it again if there is smoke or heat behind it.
steps.hint: Think about checking what is behind a closed door before the group commits to it.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: You and your colleague, with pressure still applied, have reached the bottom of the south stairwell. A shut door leads to the lobby and the exit. You checked it with the back of your hand and it is cool.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: Section S2, Checking the route, covers how to check a door before going through it and how to use doors as you move.

chat.question: How did you check the door?
chat.answer: With the back of your hand, before touching the handle. That is the check the guide describes for any door on your route.

chat.question: Why not open it wide and run through?
chat.answer: Even a cool door can hide smoke. Opening it wide leaves no chance to shut it again, and running in a group causes falls. The guide says to open a cool door slowly, ready to close it at once.

chat.question: Why not go back up and find another route?
chat.answer: A cool door means the route may be usable. Going back up takes everyone away from the exit and back towards the smoke.

chat.question: Why not wait for someone to open it?
chat.answer: Nobody may come. You can check the door yourself and keep moving.

steps.title: The call taker's questions
steps.situation: The colleague you asked to call 112 comes back to you. The call is still connected and the call taker is asking for more information. Your colleague asks whether they can hang up so they can help you.
steps.question: What do you tell them?

options.text: Hang up. Help is already on the way.
Stay on the line, answer the questions and pass on any instructions until told to hang up.
Hand the phone to the injured colleague so they can explain.

steps.why: Staying on the line lets the call taker get the details they need and give instructions until they say the call can end.
steps.hint: Think about what the call taker still needs from you, and who decides when the call ends.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: The colleague you asked to call 112 is back with you. The call is still connected, the call taker wants more information, and your colleague would like to hang up and help you.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: Section S5, Calling for help, covers the emergency number, what to say on the call and how to make sure a call is made.

chat.question: What details does the call taker need?
chat.answer: The location, what happened, the number of injured people and any hazards.

chat.question: Why not hang up once help is on the way?
chat.answer: The guide says to stay on the line until told to hang up. The call taker may still need details or have instructions for you.

chat.question: Why not give the phone to the injured colleague?
chat.answer: The injured person needs to stay still with the wound under pressure. A helper should handle the call.

chat.question: Why not put the phone down and help carry?
chat.answer: Putting the phone down loses contact with the call taker. Stay on the line until told to hang up.

steps.title: The missing person
steps.situation: A few minutes after your handover, the person who was missing walks up to the assembly point. They left the building by another exit.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: Tell the responders and the person doing the headcount at once, so the search can stop.
Wait until someone asks whether the person has turned up.
Let the person rejoin the group quietly, since they are safe now.

steps.why: The guide's handover includes any changes since. Responders may be searching for this person, so the news must reach them straight away.
steps.hint: Think about who needs this news first, and how soon.

chat.question: What is happening here?
chat.answer: You have handed over to the responders. Now the person who was missing has walked up to the assembly point; they left by another exit.

chat.question: Which part of the guide covers this?
chat.answer: S4 covers what to do at the assembly point. S10 covers the handover to the people who take over.

chat.question: Where should the group wait?
chat.answer: At the assembly point, away from the building and its entrances, so emergency teams can get in and work.

chat.question: Why not wait until someone asks?
chat.answer: Responders may be searching for this person right now. The guide's handover includes any changes since, so tell them straight away.

chat.question: Why not let them rejoin the group quietly?
chat.answer: Then nobody in charge knows, and a search could continue inside the building and put responders at risk.

chat.question: Why not send them back to find the responders?
chat.answer: The guide says not to re-enter the building until it is declared safe.
